es.title: Hackean un sistema de la CIA: qué se sabe y el papel de ARTEX
es.description: La CIA y la ODNI confirman la intrusión en un sistema no clasificado de inteligencia de fuentes abiertas. Qué se sabe, qué no y por qué apunta a ARTEX.
es.seoDescription: Brecha en la CIA: hackean un sistema no clasificado de inteligencia de fuentes abiertas. Qué se sabe, qué no, el papel de ARTEX y por qué importa.
es.body:
La CIA y la Oficina del Director de Inteligencia Nacional (ODNI) de Estados Unidos han descubierto que alguien entró en uno de sus sistemas. No es un sistema clasificado: es el que usan sus analistas para trabajar con información pública y comercial, lo que se conoce como inteligencia de fuentes abiertas u OSINT. Lo adelantó The New York Times el martes 24 de noviembre y lo han confirmado fuentes a [AP](https://apnews.com/article/cia-cyberattack-unclassified-system-bfa6d3b02e3b0e2779dfb613c900bd77), [Reuters](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/us-cia-odni-suffer-cybersecurity-breach-of-some-unclassified-information-nyt-reports-5048922) y [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/11/cia-odni-unclassified-intelligence-system-hacked/417438/). La investigación apunta, sin confirmar, a ARTEX, la herramienta de IA que ataca sola de la que ya hablé aquí.

## Lo que se sabe

- El sistema afectado sirve para analizar información pública y comercial: noticias, redes sociales o imágenes de satélite, según [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/11/cia-odni-unclassified-intelligence-system-hacked/417438/).
- No hay información clasificada afectada y el problema está resuelto, según la fuente que habló con [AP](https://apnews.com/article/cia-cyberattack-unclassified-system-bfa6d3b02e3b0e2779dfb613c900bd77).
- La ODNI dijo a [Reuters](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/us-cia-odni-suffer-cybersecurity-breach-of-some-unclassified-information-nyt-reports-5048922) que no ha habido "interrupciones en capacidades críticas ni en sistemas clasificados".
- Según The New York Times, citado por [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/11/cia-odni-unclassified-intelligence-system-hacked/417438/), también se vio afectada a la vez la Agencia Nacional de Inteligencia Geoespacial (NGA).
- La CIA no ha querido comentar, según [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/11/cia-odni-unclassified-intelligence-system-hacked/417438/).

## ARTEX, otra vez

Según [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/11/cia-odni-unclassified-intelligence-system-hacked/417438/), se cree que en el ataque se usó ARTEX, una herramienta de IA creada por un ingeniero chino conocido como "Autumn-27" que encuentra y explota fallos en sistemas sin que nadie la dirija paso a paso. El mismo medio cuenta, citando a dos personas, que ARTEX también se usó hace poco para entrar en el Mando de Ciberdefensa del Departamento de Defensa, aunque una de ellas dice que esa intrusión tuvo poco impacto.

Ojo con sacar conclusiones: que se usara ARTEX no dice quién está detrás. La herramienta circula entre delincuentes de muchos países, así que no sirve para señalar a China ni a nadie. Si quieres entender cómo funciona, lo conté en [el caso ARTEX](/es/blog/agentes-ia-ataques-automatizados-artex).

## Por qué importa aunque no sea clasificado

Que la información sea pública no quiere decir que el robo no tenga valor. Lo interesante no son los datos en sí, sino lo que buscan los analistas. Ben Bernstein, de la empresa de ciberseguridad Huntress, explicó a [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/11/cia-odni-unclassified-intelligence-system-hacked/417438/) que ver qué temas siguen y qué consultan da una idea muy clara de las prioridades y los puntos ciegos de la inteligencia de EE. UU., sin tocar un solo archivo clasificado.

Es lo mismo que pasa en una empresa: el historial de búsquedas de tu equipo de compras o de I+D dice mucho de tus planes aunque cada página consultada sea pública.

## Lo que no se sabe todavía

- Quién lo hizo. Nadie lo ha atribuido oficialmente, según [AP](https://apnews.com/article/cia-cyberattack-unclassified-system-bfa6d3b02e3b0e2779dfb613c900bd77) y [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/11/cia-odni-unclassified-intelligence-system-hacked/417438/).
- Si se llevaron información y cuál. [Reuters](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/us-cia-odni-suffer-cybersecurity-breach-of-some-unclassified-information-nyt-reports-5048922) dice que no está claro qué material se ha visto comprometido.
- Cómo entraron. Ni el Times ni las fuentes oficiales lo han explicado.
- Si tiene relación con el ataque a la base de datos criminal del FBI. Dos fuentes dijeron a CNN, según recoge [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/world/2771462/cia-hit-by-hack-impacting-unclassified-information), que no parece estar relacionado.

## El contexto

Llega después de varias semanas de incidentes y caídas en organismos y empresas de EE. UU. Según [Reuters](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/us-cia-odni-suffer-cybersecurity-breach-of-some-unclassified-information-nyt-reports-5048922), en poco tiempo se han conocido una brecha en el Departamento de Agricultura, dos en el FBI e incidentes en el Pentágono y en Seguridad Nacional. A la vez, ha habido caídas como la de la red interna de la NSA, que el Gobierno atribuye a fallos técnicos y no a ataques. Lo repasé en [las caídas en cadena en EE. UU.](/es/blog/caidas-estados-unidos-microsoft-apple-gmail-nsa-ciberataque). Si la investigación concreta quién está detrás o qué se llevaron, actualizaré este artículo.

## Qué puedes sacar de esto

1. Lo "no clasificado" también se protege. Las herramientas internas de análisis, los paneles y los buscadores de tu empresa dicen mucho de lo que haces.
2. Las herramientas de ataque con IA ya no son una curiosidad de laboratorio. Parchear rápido y vigilar los accesos raros importa más que nunca.
3. Revisa qué sistemas expuestos a internet tienes, aunque te parezcan poco importantes. Suelen ser la puerta de entrada.

Si quieres que tu equipo entienda cómo atacan ahora estas herramientas y qué hacer en el día a día, es justo lo que trabajo en mis [formaciones de ciberseguridad e IA](/es/training).

Fuentes: [AP](https://apnews.com/article/cia-cyberattack-unclassified-system-bfa6d3b02e3b0e2779dfb613c900bd77), [Reuters](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/us-cia-odni-suffer-cybersecurity-breach-of-some-unclassified-information-nyt-reports-5048922), [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/11/cia-odni-unclassified-intelligence-system-hacked/417438/) y [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/world/2771462/cia-hit-by-hack-impacting-unclassified-information), que recoge la información de CNN.

en.title: CIA system hacked: what we know and where ARTEX fits in
en.description: The CIA and ODNI confirm an intrusion into an unclassified open-source intelligence system. What we know, what we don't, and why ARTEX comes up.
en.seoDescription: CIA breach: hackers got into an unclassified open-source intelligence system. What we know, what we don't, the ARTEX link and why it matters.
en.body:
The CIA and the US Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) have found that someone broke into one of their systems. It isn't a classified system: it's the one their analysts use to work with public and commercial information, known as open-source intelligence or OSINT. The New York Times broke the story on Tuesday, November 24, and sources have confirmed it to [AP](https://apnews.com/article/cia-cyberattack-unclassified-system-bfa6d3b02e3b0e2779dfb613c900bd77), [Reuters](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/us-cia-odni-suffer-cybersecurity-breach-of-some-unclassified-information-nyt-reports-5048922) and [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/11/cia-odni-unclassified-intelligence-system-hacked/417438/). The investigation points, without confirmation, to ARTEX, the AI tool that attacks on its own that I've covered here before.

## What we know

- The affected system is used to analyse public and commercial information: news, social media or satellite imagery, according to [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/11/cia-odni-unclassified-intelligence-system-hacked/417438/).
- No classified information was affected and the issue has been resolved, according to the source who spoke to [AP](https://apnews.com/article/cia-cyberattack-unclassified-system-bfa6d3b02e3b0e2779dfb613c900bd77).
- ODNI told [Reuters](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/us-cia-odni-suffer-cybersecurity-breach-of-some-unclassified-information-nyt-reports-5048922) there had been "no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems".
- According to The New York Times, as cited by [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/11/cia-odni-unclassified-intelligence-system-hacked/417438/), the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA) was affected at the same time.
- The CIA declined to comment, according to [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/11/cia-odni-unclassified-intelligence-system-hacked/417438/).

## ARTEX, again

According to [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/11/cia-odni-unclassified-intelligence-system-hacked/417438/), ARTEX is believed to have been used in the attack. It's an AI tool built by a Chinese engineer known as "Autumn-27" that finds and exploits flaws in systems without anyone guiding it step by step. The same outlet reports, citing two people, that ARTEX was also recently used to break into the Defense Department's Cyber Defense Command, although one of them says that intrusion had little impact.

Be careful with conclusions: the use of ARTEX doesn't tell you who's behind it. The tool is used by criminals in many countries, so it can't be used to point at China or anyone else. If you want to understand how it works, I covered it in [the ARTEX case](/en/blog/ai-agents-automated-attacks-artex).

## Why it matters even if it isn't classified

Public information doesn't mean the theft is worthless. What's valuable isn't the data itself but what the analysts are looking for. Ben Bernstein, of cybersecurity firm Huntress, told [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/11/cia-odni-unclassified-intelligence-system-hacked/417438/) that seeing which topics they follow and what they search for gives a very clear picture of US intelligence priorities and blind spots, without touching a single classified file.

It's the same in a company: the search history of your purchasing or R&D team says a lot about your plans, even if every page they looked at is public.

## What we still don't know

- Who did it. Nobody has officially attributed it, according to [AP](https://apnews.com/article/cia-cyberattack-unclassified-system-bfa6d3b02e3b0e2779dfb613c900bd77) and [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/11/cia-odni-unclassified-intelligence-system-hacked/417438/).
- Whether information was taken, and what. [Reuters](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/us-cia-odni-suffer-cybersecurity-breach-of-some-unclassified-information-nyt-reports-5048922) says it isn't clear what material was compromised.
- How they got in. Neither the Times nor official sources have explained it.
- Whether it's linked to the attack on the FBI's criminal database. Two sources told CNN, as reported by [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/world/2771462/cia-hit-by-hack-impacting-unclassified-information), that it doesn't appear to be related.

## The context

It comes after several weeks of incidents and outages at US agencies and companies. According to [Reuters](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/us-cia-odni-suffer-cybersecurity-breach-of-some-unclassified-information-nyt-reports-5048922), in a short time there have been reports of a breach at the Department of Agriculture, two at the FBI, and incidents at the Pentagon and Homeland Security. At the same time there have been outages such as the one on the NSA's internal network, which the government blames on technical failures rather than attacks. I went through them in [the back-to-back US outages](/en/blog/us-outages-microsoft-apple-gmail-nsa-cyberattack). If the investigation establishes who's behind it or what was taken, I'll update this article.

## What you can take from this

1. "Unclassified" still needs protecting. Your company's internal analysis tools, dashboards and search tools say a lot about what you do.
2. AI attack tools are no longer a lab curiosity. Patching fast and watching for unusual access matters more than ever.
3. Check which systems you have exposed to the internet, even if they seem unimportant. They're often the way in.

If you want your team to understand how these tools attack now and what to do day to day, that's exactly what I cover in my [cybersecurity and AI training](/en/training).

Sources: [AP](https://apnews.com/article/cia-cyberattack-unclassified-system-bfa6d3b02e3b0e2779dfb613c900bd77), [Reuters](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/us-cia-odni-suffer-cybersecurity-breach-of-some-unclassified-information-nyt-reports-5048922), [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/11/cia-odni-unclassified-intelligence-system-hacked/417438/) and [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/world/2771462/cia-hit-by-hack-impacting-unclassified-information), which carries CNN's reporting.
